entry: [[Canada|Canadian]] pizza topped with [[Pineapple|pineapple]], tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and either [[Ham|ham]] or bacon. Greek-born Canadian Sam Panopoulos is credited with creating the first version in 1962 at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham-Kent, Ontario. The name refers to the canned pineapple, from the Hawaiian Pineapple Company, that he used, rather than to the U.S. state of [[Hawaii]]. Opinions are polarized; many enjoy the sweet-and-savory combination, and others vehemently dislike it. In 2017, Iceland’s president jokingly said he would ban pineapple on pizza, a remark that drew wide media coverage.

Romantic or sexual attraction, or sexual behavior, between people of the opposite sex or gender. As a [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientation]], heterosexuality is, with [[Bisexuality|bisexuality]] and [[Homosexuality|homosexuality]], one of three main categories within the heterosexual–homosexual continuum. Karl Maria Kertbeny coined the term in 1869 alongside homosexual. Across cultures, most people are heterosexual, and heterosexual activity is by far the most common type of sexual activity. Heterosexuality has mostly been viewed as the normative and most socially dominant orientation. Scientists do not know the exact cause of sexual orientation, but they theorize a complex interplay of genetic, hormonal, and environmental influences, and they favor biologically based theories. The term is usually applied to humans, but heterosexual behavior is observed in all other [[Mammal|mammals]] and in other animals, as it is necessary for [[Sexual reproduction|sexual reproduction]].

[[Rail transport]] network with trains significantly faster than traditional rail, on specialized [[Rolling stock|rolling stock]] and dedicated tracks. Lines built for at least 250 km/h, or upgraded lines of at least 200 km/h, are generally considered high-speed, though no single worldwide definition exists. The first dedicated system, the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, began operations in [[Honshu]], [[Japan]], in October 1964; its trains, known in English as bullet trains, could maintain 210 km/h. The United States began Metroliner services at 200 km/h in 1969. Japan’s dedicated-track model was followed by several European countries, initially Italy, then [[France]], [[Germany]], and Spain. Since the 21st century, [[China]] has taken a leading role, and by 2023 its network accounted for over two-thirds of the world’s total. High-speed rail is the fastest and most efficient ground-based method of commercial transport, though construction is costlier than conventional rail and does not always offer an economic advantage.

Complete abstract [[Vector space|vector space]] with an [[Inner product space|inner product]] allowing length and angle to be measured. It generalizes [[Euclidean space]] to spaces of any finite or infinite dimension, extending the methods of Euclidean geometry and calculus. Hilbert spaces were studied beginning in the first decade of the 20th century by [[David Hilbert]], after whom they are named, together with Erhard Schmidt and Frigyes Riesz. [[John von Neumann]] coined the term for the abstract concept. They are indispensable in partial differential equations, [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], Fourier analysis, signal processing, heat transfer, and ergodic theory. Examples include spaces of square-integrable functions and sequence spaces, and completeness ensures that enough limits exist for the techniques of calculus to be used.

Human and political history of the [[Australia (continent)|Australian continent]], from the arrival of the first [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal Australian]] ancestors 50,000 to 65,000 years ago to the present multicultural democracy. The Commonwealth of Australia was proclaimed on January 1, 1901, as a federation of six self-governing former British colonies. In 1770, [[James Cook]] charted the east coast and claimed it for Great Britain. The [[First Fleet]] arrived at [[Sydney]] Cove in January 1788 and established a penal colony. In the following century, colonization brought introduced diseases, violent conflict, and dispossession that reduced the Aboriginal population, while gold rushes and agriculture brought prosperity. Australia fought in both world wars as part of the British Empire and became a long-standing ally of the United States through the [[Cold War]]. Post-war immigration brought more than 7 million migrants, and the population exceeded 25.5 million by 2021, with 30 percent born overseas.

Development of [[Cryptography|codes and ciphers]] from antiquity onward. The earliest known deliberate transformation of a text is in non-standard hieroglyphs carved into a tomb wall from the [[Old Kingdom of Egypt]], c. 1900 BC. Frequency analysis, a method of [[Cryptanalysis|cryptanalysis]], on occasion altered the course of history, as when it was applied to the Zimmermann Telegram, which helped trigger U.S. entry into World War I. Allied reading of ciphers from [[Nazi Germany]] shortened World War II, by as much as two years in some evaluations.

Development of the description and mapping of the Earth, from ancient practices to a distinct academic discipline. The first person to use the word [[Geography|geography]], from Greek for “Earth-writing,” was [[Eratosthenes]], though mapping and other practices predate the term. The oldest known world maps date to ancient [[Babylon]] from the 9th century BC. The best-known Babylonian map, the Imago Mundi of about 600 BC, shows Babylon on the Euphrates within a circular landmass ringed by a “bitter river.” The Greeks regarded [[Homer]] as the founder of geography, and [[Anaximander]] is the first known person to have attempted a scale map of the known world. [[Herodotus]]’ *Histories*, though primarily a work of history, contains a wealth of geographic description. In 19th-century Germany, [[Alexander von Humboldt]] and [[Carl Ritter]] helped establish geography as a university discipline.

Development of organized physical competition and games, from prehistoric activity to the modern era. Early sport was linked with warfare and entertainment, and competition was used to determine whether individuals were fit for military service. Wrestlers are depicted on [[Sumer|Sumerian]] stone slabs dated to around 3000 BC, and Egyptian monuments at Beni Hasan from around 2000 BC show wrestling, weightlifting, long jump, rowing, and archery. The first recorded [[Olympic Games]] were held at Olympia in 776 BC and celebrated until 393 AD; the four-year cycle became a unit of time in historical chronologies. The *Iliad* describes funeral games for fallen warriors. [[Cricket|Cricket]] and [[Association football|association football]] gained standardized rules in the 19th century, and [[Pierre de Coubertin]] revived the Olympic Games in modern times.

Current geological epoch, the youngest division of the [[Quaternary]] period, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago as the [[Last Glacial Period]] ended. It is an interglacial period within the ongoing glacial cycles of the Quaternary and is often called the Age of Humans, as it corresponds with the rapid growth and impact of the human species, including the rise of major civilizations and urban living. Its ecosystems continue to be affected by the [[Holocene extinction]], largely of human causation. In 2018, the International Union of Geological Sciences divided the epoch into three ages on climatic grounds: the Greenlandian, the Northgrippian, and the Meghalayan, the last of which began with an extreme drought lasting around 200 years. Proposals to define a succeeding [[Anthropocene]] epoch remain unratified by international stratigraphic authorities.

Playground game popular in many countries, played by tossing a small marker into numbered squares and hopping through the court to retrieve it. Courts are scratched in dirt or drawn in [[Chalk|chalk]] on pavement, usually as linear squares with a “safe” or “home” base at the end. Single squares are hopped on one foot and paired squares straddled with both feet. A turn ends if a player steps on a line, misses a square, or loses balance, and the first player to complete the course for every numbered square wins. The game is both a physical and cognitive workout. Its origin is unknown, and there is no evidence that it existed before the 16th century; the first English references, from the late 17th century, call it “scotch-hop.”

Russian former intelligence officer and militant leader. He led the April 2014 seizure of Sloviansk, which he later described as the spark of the Donbas War, and was briefly defense minister of the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic. In 2022 a Dutch court convicted him in absentia of murder over the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17; he acknowledged “moral responsibility” but denied pushing the button. Russian authorities convicted him in January 2024 of inciting extremism after he publicly criticized [[Vladimir Putin]].

Name given to several real and fictitious groups, most often the [[Bavaria|Bavarian]] Illuminati, an Enlightenment-era secret society founded on May 1, 1776, to oppose superstition and abuses of state power. Charles Theodore, Elector of Bavaria, outlawed it in 1784 and later years, with the encouragement of the [[Catholic Church]]. Conservative and religious critics later claimed that it continued underground and was responsible for the [[French Revolution]]. Later conspiracy theories depict the Illuminati as secretly controlling world affairs, though links between later organizations and the original society are unsubstantiated.

Chemical element of atomic number 49 (symbol In), a silvery-white [[Post-transition metal|post-transition metal]] and one of the softest elements. Chemically it is intermediate between [[Gallium|gallium]] and [[Thallium|thallium]]. Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter discovered it in 1863 by spectroscopic methods and named it for the indigo-blue line in its spectrum. It is used mainly in [[Flat-panel display|flat-panel displays]] as indium tin oxide, a transparent conductive coating on glass. It is also used in [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]], low-melting [[Solder|solders]], and blue and white LED circuits. It is produced exclusively as a [[By-product|by-product]] of processing other metal ores, chiefly zinc sulfide ores. It has no biological role, and its compounds are toxic when inhaled or injected into the bloodstream.

American-born dancer and choreographer, a pioneer of [[Modern dance]]. Born and raised in California, she lived and performed in Western Europe, the United States, and Soviet Russia. She rejected the rigid technique of [[Ballet|ballet]] in favor of natural, fluid movement, dancing barefoot in loose, flowing garments and drawing inspiration from Greek vases and sculptures in the [[British Museum]]. In 1902 she began touring Europe with [[Loie Fuller]], and she spent much of the rest of her life touring Europe and the Americas. Her distinctive style influenced visual artists, including [[Auguste Rodin]], Antoine Bourdelle, and Abraham Walkowitz. She established dance schools in Berlin, Paris, and Moscow to train pupils in her method. She died in Nice, France, when her long scarf became entangled in the wheel of an open car.

Canadian and New Zealand filmmaker and explorer. Born and raised in Ontario, Canada, he moved to California at 17 and first gained recognition for writing and directing *The Terminator* (1984). His films, including *Aliens* (1986), *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* (1991), and *Titanic* (1997), combine cutting-edge technology with classical filmmaking and have grossed over $10 billion worldwide, making him the second highest-grossing film director of all time. *Titanic* won [[Academy Awards]] for Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing. Three of his films have been selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]]. As a [[National Geographic]] explorer-in-residence, he has produced documentaries on deep-ocean exploration. In 2012 he became the first person to complete a solo descent to the bottom of the [[Mariana Trench]] in the *Deepsea Challenger* submersible.

American retired actress and Academy Award winner. She made her breakthrough in the 1950s, playing complex women with nuance and depth of character. Her performance as a woman with [[Dissociative identity disorder]] in *The Three Faces of Eve* (1957) earned her the Academy Award for Best Actress. She was married to actor [[Paul Newman]] for fifty years, until his death, and they often worked together. Her accolades include three Primetime [[Emmy Awards]]. She is the oldest living Best Actress Oscar winner.

English heavy metal band formed in [[Birmingham]] in 1969. The band has sold over 50 million albums and is frequently ranked among the greatest metal bands of all time. Its sixth studio album, *British Steel* (1980), brought mainstream attention, and *The Guardian* described it as the record that defines heavy metal. The band is cited as an influence on [[Thrash metal|thrash]], speed, and power metal. Glenn Tipton has limited his touring since 2018 because of [[Parkinson's disease]]. In 2022 the band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Marginal sea of the [[Arctic Ocean]] north of [[Siberia]], separated from the [[Barents Sea]] to the west by the Kara Strait and Novaya Zemlya, and from the [[Laptev Sea]] to the east by the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago. It is roughly 1,450 km long and 970 km wide, with an area of about 880,000 sq km and a mean depth of 110 m. Its main ports are Novy Port and Dikson. The sea is an important fishing ground but is ice-bound for all but two months of the year. It contains the East-Prinovozemelsky field, an extension of the West Siberian Oil Basin with significant undeveloped [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and [[Natural gas|natural gas]]. The name derives from the Kara River, which played a role in the Russian conquest of northern Siberia.

Capital and largest city of [[Tatarstan]], Russia, at the confluence of the [[Volga]] and Kazanka rivers. Kazan was the capital of the [[Khanate of Kazan]] until [[Ivan the Terrible]] conquered it in the 16th century, after which it became part of the [[Tsardom of Russia]]. The city was seized and largely destroyed during Pugachev’s Rebellion (1773–75) and was rebuilt under [[Catherine the Great]]. In 1920 it became the capital of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, and after the dissolution of the [[Soviet Union]] it remained the capital of Tatarstan. Kazan is known for its mix of Tatar and Russian cultures, and the Kazan Kremlin is a [[World Heritage Site]]. The city hosted the 2013 Summer Universiade and was one of the host cities of the 2018 World Cup.

Disputed [[Super-Earth|super-Earth]] [[Exoplanet|exoplanet]] candidate orbiting the Sun-like star Kepler-452, about 1,800 light-years away in the constellation [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]]. The [[Kepler space telescope]] found it, and NASA announced the discovery on July 23, 2015. Two later reports refuted the claim, but additional work has reestablished it. It orbits in about 385 days at 1.04 astronomical units, and its radius is about 1.63 times Earth’s. It is the first potentially rocky super-Earth found in the [[Habitable zone|habitable zone]] of a very Sun-like star, though whether it is habitable is unknown.

Colored varieties of [[Carp|carp]] kept for decorative purposes in outdoor ponds and water gardens. Known formally in Japanese as *nishikigoi*, or “brocaded carp,” they were first bred in [[Niigata Prefecture|Niigata]], Japan, in the early 19th century. Varieties are distinguished by coloration, patterning, and scalation, with major colors including white, black, red, orange, yellow, blue, brown, and cream, as well as metallic gold and silver-white scales. The most popular category is the Gosanke, made up of the *Kōhaku*, *Taishō Sanshoku*, and *Shōwa Sanshoku* varieties. Carp were domesticated in China for food and reached Japan later; the [[Nihon Shoki]] (720) records Emperor Keikō releasing carp into a pond for viewing. Released into non-native waterways, koi can become an [[Invasive species|invasive species]] that increases turbidity and displaces native fish.

Lake in the central [[Taymyr Peninsula]], Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia, south of the [[Byrranga Mountains]]. It is about 165 km long, with an irregular shape and many arms, and it is ice-covered from late September until June. Fish include loach, common whitefish, and muksun, and some species are [[Overexploitation|overexploited]]. Slight [[Plutonium|plutonium]] contamination found in its sediments is possibly a result of wind-carried particles from atmospheric nuclear tests at [[Novaya Zemlya]] during the [[Cold War]].

Jawless fish of the order Petromyzontiformes, with a toothed, funnel-like sucking [[Mouth|mouth]]. About 38 living species are known, classified in three families, one large family in the Northern Hemisphere and two small ones in the Southern. Genetic evidence places lampreys closer to [[Hagfish|hagfish]] than to jawed [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], and the oldest stem-group fossils date from the latest [[Devonian]], about 360 million years ago. Most lampreys spend much of their lives as larvae, called ammocoetes, that burrow into sediment and filter-feed. Only 18 species are carnivorous as adults, boring into other fish to consume flesh and blood, and nonparasitic adults do not feed. The [[Sea lamprey|sea lamprey]] has become a significant introduced pest in the [[Great Lakes]], where control programs use lampricides and barriers.

Period of societal collapse across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the late 13th to early 12th century BC. The palace economies of [[Mycenaean Greece]] and Anatolia broke apart into small village cultures of the [[Greek Dark Ages]], which lasted from about 1200 BC to 800 BC. The Hittite Empire collapsed, while states such as the Middle Assyrian Empire and the [[New Kingdom of Egypt]] survived in weakened forms, and the Phoenicians gained autonomy. Proposed causes since the 19th century include climate change, drought, disease, invasions by the [[Sea Peoples]], and changes in military technology that brought the decline of [[Chariot|chariot]] warfare. Later scholarship has argued that the collapse was more limited than once thought: Jesse Millek found that 94 of 153 reported destruction events around 1200 BC were misdated, assumed on little evidence, or never happened.

Activity invoking the power of a [[Court|tribunal]] to enforce a law. Legal proceedings are generally orderly, with participants presenting [[Evidence (law)|evidence]] before a [[Judge|judge]] or [[Jury|jury]] that determines the facts and legal issues. They include [[Trial|trials]], enforcement of court orders, hearings, and arbitration. A civil case begins when a [[Plaintiff]] files a [[Complaint]] seeking a remedy such as money or an injunction. In the United States, [[Impeachment|impeachment]] proceedings are generally conducted as legal proceedings, though experts dispute whether they are primarily political.
